prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map depicts a living room viewed from an elevated egocentric angle, showing a couch along the left wall (~1.5 to 3.5 m away), a coffee table along the right (~2 to 3.5 m away), a TV stand and shelving at the far back (~3.5 to 4 m away), and a child seated centrally on the floor rug surrounded by puzzle box halves (~0.2 to 0.8 m from the child) and a pillow ~1 m to the child's left. Across the five frames, the camera wearer walks forward and tilts the camera steeply downward toward the child—who remains seated facing away toward the TV and never looks toward the camera wearer—reducing the camera-to-child distance from ~2.5–3 m in frame 1 to ~2 m in frame 2, ~1.5 m in frame 3, ~1 m in frame 4, and ~0.7 m directly below the camera in frame 5. The camera wearer's own hands and lower limbs partially visible at the bottom edge (~0.3 to 0.5 m away in frames 1–3 and 5) and the near end of the left couch in frames 1–3 are within the wearer's arm's reach, while by frame 5 the child is also within the wearer's reach, and the puzzle boxes and scattered pieces on the floor remain within the child's arm's reach (~0.3 to 0.5 m around the child) as the upper walls and far furniture progressively exit the top and sides of the view. Compared to the RGB strip alone, the continuous luminance gradients clearly separate the 3D elevation of the child's head and torso, the raised rims of the puzzle boxes on the busy patterned rug, and the changing tilt of the floor plane relative to the viewer. However, the depth map is unreliable in frames 1–3 where the dark TV stand and rear shelves (~3.5 to 4 m away) saturate to uniform black with no internal geometry, and in frame 4 where the child's torso and legs blend into nearly the same mid-grey depth value as the surrounding floor.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates only a sparse subset of foreground objects against a black background across the five frames: the left couch (~1.5 to 3.5 m away) in frame 1, the far TV (~3.5 m ahead) and seated child (~2 m ahead in the center) in frame 2, the child (~1.5 m ahead) plus the camera wearer's own pointing left hand/arm and legs at the bottom edge (~0.3 to 0.5 m away) in frame 3, no objects at all in frame 4, and the child plus the wearer's lower legs at the bottom (~0.5 to 0.8 m below) in frame 5. In the frames where the child is detected (frames 2, 3, and 5), the masks show the child positioned on the floor below and in front of the approaching camera wearer, facing away toward the top of the image without looking toward the camera wearer, with arms extended toward the floor within a ~0.3 to 0.5 m reach, while the wearer's own segmented limbs at the bottom of frames 3 and 5 lie within the wearer's immediate reach (~0.3 to 0.6 m). Where masks do appear in frames 2 and 3, their silhouettes separate the 2D contour of the child's upper body and the wearer's pointing finger from the visually busy, high-contrast floral rug pattern more starkly than the RGB image alone. However, the map is largely unreliable for scene layout: it misclassifies the partially cut-off left couch as a "teddy bear" in frame 1, splits the TV into two masks in frame 2, fragments the wearer's partly visible limbs at the bottom of frame 3 into three separate "person" instances, merges the child and the wearer's legs at the bottom of frame 5 into a single "person" mask, misses the child completely in frames 1 and 4, and fails to segment the coffee table, shelves, and nearby puzzle boxes (~0.2 to 0.8 m from the child) in every frame.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is blank across almost the entire living room sequence, detecting only a yellow upper-body and head skeleton for the seated child near the center of frame 3 (~1.5 m in front of and below the camera wearer) and a small magenta cluster of hand keypoints on the child's right hand in frame 5 (~0.7 m below the camera and slightly right of center). In frame 3, the yellow shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints span roughly 0.5 m horizontally below the head keypoints without frontal facial landmarks oriented toward the viewer, showing the child seated facing away from the camera wearer with both arms outstretched within arm's reach (~0.3 to 0.4 m) of the surrounding floor and puzzle pieces, while in frame 5 the magenta keypoints locate the child's right hand resting on the rug within arm's reach of both the child and the overhead camera wearer. Compared to the RGB strip, the frame 3 skeleton explicitly isolates the child's shoulder and elbow joint articulation against the camouflaging rug pattern, and the frame 5 hand skeleton pinpoints the exact finger cluster on the floor during the steep top-down close-up. However, the pose map is highly unreliable across the sequence because it fails to detect the child's body in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5 as the camera approaches from ~2.5 m to ~0.7 m and pitches steeply downward, omits the child's legs in frame 3, provides no representation of the surrounding furniture or puzzle boxes, and completely misses the camera wearer's own partially visible hands and legs at the bottom edge of frames 1, 2, 3, and 5.
